course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

topic.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
topic.summary: Arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent: why the trigonometric functions need restricted domains to be invertible, which domains are used, and how the output of an inverse trigonometric function is read as an angle.

questions.prompt: What is the value of arcsin(1/2)?
questions.explanation: arcsin(1/2) is the angle in [−π/2, π/2] whose sine is 1/2, which is π/6.
choiceExplanations: sin(5π/6) = 1/2, but 5π/6 is outside the range [−π/2, π/2] of arcsine.
π/6 is in [−π/2, π/2] and sin(π/6) = 1/2.
30 is the degree measure; arcsine returns radians here.
questions.distinguisher: Arcsine returns only angles in [−π/2, π/2].

questions.prompt: What is the value of arccos(−1/2)?
questions.explanation: arccos(−1/2) is the angle in [0, π] whose cosine is −1/2. That is 2π/3, in Quadrant II.
choiceExplanations: Arccosine's outputs are between 0 and π, so they are never negative.
2π/3 is in [0, π] and cos(2π/3) = −1/2.
cos(4π/3) = −1/2, but 4π/3 is outside [0, π].
Outputs of arccosine are never negative.
questions.distinguisher: Arccosine of a negative value is an angle in Quadrant II, not a negative angle.

questions.prompt: What is the range of y = arctan x?
questions.explanation: Tangent is restricted to (−π/2, π/2), an open interval because tangent is undefined at ±π/2. The range of the inverse is that same interval.
choiceExplanations: ±π/2 are not included, because tangent has asymptotes there.
0 ≤ y ≤ π is the range of arccosine.
The open interval (−π/2, π/2).
All real numbers is the domain of arctangent, its inputs.
questions.distinguisher: The tangent's restricted domain is open.

questions.prompt: Why must the domain of the sine function be restricted in order to define the arcsine function?
choices: Because sine has vertical asymptotes that must be removed
Because sine is periodic, so it is not one-to-one
Because the range of sine is all real numbers
Because sine is undefined for negative angles
questions.explanation: Because the trigonometric functions are periodic, they are only invertible if they have restricted domains. On [−π/2, π/2], each value of sine comes from exactly one angle.
choiceExplanations: Sine has no vertical asymptotes; tangent does.
A periodic function repeats its outputs, so each output comes from infinitely many inputs.
The range of sine is −1 ≤ y ≤ 1.
The domain of sine is all real numbers.
questions.distinguisher: Invertible means one-to-one, and periodic functions are not.

questions.prompt: What is the value of arcsin(sin(5π/6))?
questions.explanation: sin(5π/6) = 1/2, and arcsin(1/2) = π/6, the angle in [−π/2, π/2] with sine 1/2.
choiceExplanations: 5π/6 is outside the range of arcsine, so the composition cannot return it.
1/2 is sin(5π/6), the inside value, not the final output.
arcsin(1/2) = π/6.
questions.distinguisher: arcsin(sin θ) = θ only when θ is in [−π/2, π/2].

questions.prompt: What is the domain of y = arccos x?
questions.explanation: The inputs of arccosine are values of cosine, which lie in [−1, 1].
choiceExplanations: Inputs are values in the range of cosine.
0 ≤ y ≤ π is the range of arccosine, its outputs.
Only arctangent accepts all real numbers.
This is the restricted domain of sine.
questions.distinguisher: Inverse inputs are the original function's outputs.

questions.prompt: What is the value of arctan(−√3)?
choiceExplanations: tan(2π/3) = −√3, but 2π/3 is outside the range of arctangent.
−π/3 is in (−π/2, π/2) and has tangent −√3.
tan(π/3) = √3, which has the wrong sign.
questions.distinguisher: Arctangent of a negative value is a negative angle.

questions.prompt: Let θ = arcsin(3/5). What is the value of cos θ?
questions.explanation: θ is in [−π/2, π/2] with sin θ = 3/5 > 0, so θ is in Quadrant I. On a circle of radius 5, the point is (4, 3), so cos θ = 4/5.
choiceExplanations: Arcsine outputs are in [−π/2, π/2], where cosine is never negative.
3/4 is tan θ.
Cosine values never exceed 1.
θ is in Quadrant I, and 3² + 4² = 5².
questions.distinguisher: The range of arcsine fixes the sign of the cosine.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes the graph of y = arccos x?
choices: It increases from (−1, 0) to (1, π) through (0, π/2).
It decreases from (−1, π) to (1, 0), passing through (0, π/2).
It has horizontal asymptotes y = 0 and y = π.
questions.explanation: Cosine decreases on [0, π] from 1 to −1, so its inverse decreases from arccos(−1) = π to arccos(1) = 0.
choiceExplanations: This reverses the points; arccos(−1) = π, not 0.
arccos(−1) = π and arccos(1) = 0.
Arccosine's outputs are between 0 and π.
Arccosine is defined only on [−1, 1], so it has no end behavior and no horizontal asymptotes.
questions.distinguisher: Cosine decreases on [0, π], so arccosine decreases too.

questions.prompt: A wheelchair ramp rises 1.2 meters over a horizontal distance of 6 meters. Which of the following gives the angle θ, in radians, between the ramp and the ground?
questions.explanation: The slope of the ramp is tan θ = 1.2/6 = 0.2. The angle is the output of the inverse: θ = arctan(0.2) ≈ 0.197.
choiceExplanations: tan θ = 0.2, so θ = arctan(0.2).
1/tan(0.2) is neither the angle nor the slope.
tan(0.2) treats 0.2 as an angle, but 0.2 is the slope.
0.2 is rise over run, which is the tangent; the sine would be rise over the ramp's length.
questions.distinguisher: The given ratio is a tangent, so use arctangent.
